THE SYMBOLS OVER THE SYSTEM AND FAN LAMPS, and the small legends over the console and management jacks. They are printed in blue at about two pixels' height and are not legible in the figure; PS1 and PS2 are. Guide figures A-1 and A-2 say the lamps are labelled in one of two ways and the held figure does not say which this chassis uses.
A LAMP AND A BLUE SYMBOL ABOVE THE ToD CONNECTOR (about 428.9 and 434.8 mm, 34.3 mm down). Figure C-2 draws them and no callout or table names them. They are not modelled.

WHETHER THE PPS AND 10MHZ JACKS ARE SMB OR SMA. The guide calls them "E-Sync clock connectors" and the data sheet "PPS/10M/ToD inputs"; neither names the connector. They are seated as std/smb@1 from their drawn size and their direction (input or output) is not stated either.

THE USB GENERATION. The guide says "USB port" and the data sheet "USB Ports 1"; neither gives a generation, and figure C-2 draws a gold tongue, which is neither USB-IF colour. The port is seated with the `usb2` (white) skin as the one that claims least; a data sheet line giving the generation closes it.

A BLACK ROUND HOLE at the left end, 4.8 mm from the edge and 53.4 mm down, in line with the strips. Figure C-2 draws it and nothing names it (an ESD socket is a candidate on other switches). It is drawn as a hole in decor and carries no part.

THE PRINTING AT THE REAR. The ground strip prints three symbols and the rear carries the airflow marks, but the guide's rear panel figure is 1.19 px/mm and its labels are unreadable. The supplies and fans print no numbers that resolve. A rear photograph closes it.

THE PWR-2411-DC FACE. The guide shows the PWR-1900-DC and PWR-500-DC (figure 4-5) and no PWR-2411-DC. Table 7 note 2 says its terminals are "twin #10 studs spaced for dual-hole lug with 5/8 inch hole spacing"; the supply here is the AC housing with a plain two-pole block, and the protective earth terminal "on the opposite side" is not drawn. The data sheet reads "AWG #6 Max" for the DC input connector and table 7 reads 2 to 4 AWG; the larger conductor (the guide's) is the one a lug takes.

THE KITS, AND THE EAR POSITION THAT IS NOT FLUSH. `chassis.ears` states the one position the guide names for a 2RU switch: section 3.5 says the bracket sits "either flush with the front and rear panels, or not flush with the panels", and section 3.4 gives no two-post mounting for the 2RU switches, so the position is `4-post` only. It has no `at` (the guide's mounting figures are isometric drawings of other switches, the 7050 and the 7050SX-128), no `default` (no figure shows the ears as shipped) and the "not flush" case is left out because the guide does not say which way it sits. The data sheet's ordering information lists KIT-7202 (spare tool-free accessory kit v2 for 2RU, 4-post mount, 2x C19-C20) and KIT-7004-2UL (extended tool-free 4-post kit for 2-4RU) for the DR3A-36. Guide appendix B.1 gives KIT-7202 "rack depths of twenty two to thirty two inches" (558.8 to 812.8 mm) and its parts (ASY-06132 rack ear, ASY-03765 front rail, ASY-03767 rear sliding rail, two of each), but no document dimensions any of those parts, and none gives KIT-7004-2UL a range or a parts list. A kit contract needs its parts as components with a size, so neither kit is modelled and `chassis.kits` is left out.
THE POWER DRAW OF FAN-7012H. Neither the guide nor the data sheet gives it. The supplies' own output (2400 W) is stated and is written.

gaps.note: The BDM2/BDM2m datasheet states "Total Power 300 W" in a technical specifications table headed "BDM2/2 m with 6+12 IO Card", whose RF connector row describes that card's six downstream and twelve upstream ports. The figure is the assembly's. A BDM position is TWO modules here - casa/bdm in a front bay and casa/io-6p12 in the paired rear bay, which is why casa/bdm already carries `pairs-with` - and no document we hold divides the 300 W between them. Writing it onto the front module would make the chassis total come out right and the answer to "what does a BDM front module draw" come out wrong, so neither half carries a figure and the chassis total stays a floor. The arithmetic does not settle it either way: 12 x 300 W lands on the C100G's stated 3.6 kW whether the 300 W is the pair or the front half with small rear cards. The C100G HIG corroborates the assembly reading and hedges it: Tables A-10 and A-11 both read "Approximately 300W per BDM" under titles scoping them to the BDM WITH its 6+12 I/O. THE LIBRARY IS CURRENTLY INCONSISTENT ABOUT THIS, ON PURPOSE AND VISIBLY. The three BDM variants carry NO power figure, for the reason above. The DQM and DCU cards added later DO carry one - DS8x8 220, DS8x96 320, DS8x192 350, US16x8 220, US16x4 150 - each with a `power-scope` provenance entry saying in the vendor's own words that the number covers the card WITH its I/O module and must not have a rear figure added to it. Both are defensible readings of the same problem: one keeps the per-module answer honest and the chassis total a floor, the other keeps the vendor's only published number reachable. They should not stay different once a pairing-scoped mechanism exists, and this is the record of which way each went and why, so that whoever unifies them is not guessing. THE THREE REAR RF I/O CARDS ADDED LATER FALL ON THE SAME SIDE OF THIS AS THE 6+12. casa/rfd, casa/rfu-16x8 and casa/ups-32x4 carry NO power figure, because Tables A-8 and A-9 give their port counts and connector types and no watts at all, and every figure Casa does publish for the slot is already the pair's - Table A-3 heads the DQM column "Maximum consumption with I/O module" and Table A-4 gives "Single DCU w/ RFU I/O" 200 W against "Single DCU w/ RFU UPS 32x4 I/O" 220 W for the same US16x8. Subtracting one from the other to get a rear card's share would be our arithmetic and would also be the wrong subtraction - the 20 W is the difference between two PAIRINGS, not between two I/O cards.
gaps.wanted: a pairable unit that can carry properties, so that a figure measured on a pair can be attached to the pair. The scope is now DATA - every card here declares `power-draw-scope: module-with-paired-io`, so a chassis sum knows not to add the rear partner and L30 catches it if one gains its own figure - but the scope says only THAT the figure covers a pair, not WHICH pair. The C100G HIG gives the same US16x8 200 W with the RFU I/O and 220 W with the RFU UPS 32x4, and the manifest can carry only one of them. Asking for "a per-module figure" was the wrong question: Casa states none, and one may not exist to be divided out. What is missing is the mechanism, and enough vendors doing this to design one from - Casa is the only one in the corpus.

gaps.note: The HIG body text states "Each fan assembly module has a maximum power consumption of 100W, totaling 300W across the three fan assemblies". Table A-2 of the same guide gives the row "Fan assembly (3)" as "330W maximum, 220W typical". Both are about the set of three and 300 is not 330. The contract takes 100 W because it is the only figure stated PER MODULE, which is the granularity a bay occupant needs; dividing 330 by three would be our arithmetic, not the vendor's. A chassis total is therefore 30 W light against the guide's own set figure, and no per-module typical exists at all.
gaps.wanted: a measurement from a running chassis, a vendor erratum, or a later revision of the guide that drops one of the two figures

gaps.note: Casa rates a power ENTRY module in amps and volts, never in watts. gaps.note: THE ORDERING SHEET SELLS FOUR CHASSIS AND THIS LIBRARY MODELS TWO. C40G_DS_RevA lists C40G-CHASSIS-AC and C40G-CHASSIS-DC, which are here, and C40G-CHASSIS-ACR and C40G-CHASSIS-DCR, described as "with Redundant Power and Cooling", which are not. The sheet gives the phrase and nothing else - no count, no which modules, no dimensions - and the installation guide never uses the word for a chassis variant. What the guide DOES say is that the C40G takes up to four 1100 W PSUs operating concurrently and that fewer than two cannot power a C40G-20, which tells you the supplies are redundant by population rather than by chassis. That makes the R variants most likely a populated bundle rather than different metal - but "most likely" is not a source, and inventing two configurations from a four-word description would put a guess where a part number goes.
gaps.wanted: a Casa or CommScope ordering guide saying what the R bundles contain - how many PSUs and fan modules, and whether the chassis itself differs at all

gaps.note: Casa says two things about this terminal and they do not agree. The prose in "Connecting the chassis to ground" says it "provides two M6 screws to connect a double-lug ground terminal cable". Figures 1-2 and 1-4 both DRAW three studs, in a 2x2 grid with the protective-earth mark in the fourth corner, and the two figures agree with each other. THE DRAWING IS FOLLOWED, and the model carries three. The figure is the only source that says anything about arrangement at all, so following the prose would mean inventing a layout for the two it describes; and a third stud has easy explanations - a spare, an alternate lug pitch - while a stud drawn twice that is not there has none. That is a judgement, not a reading, which is why it is filed here. THE PITCH IS NOT MEASURED FROM EITHER. It is borrowed from casa/ground-bolts@1, 15.3, off the maintainer`s hand-built C100G rear SVG. Figure 1-4 gives 13.2 across and 14.7 down for what must be one square grid - an 11 percent disagreement with itself, which is that figure`s anisotropy rather than a rectangular pattern. THE LUG THE GUIDE NAMES POINTS AT 5/8 IN. AND AT A REASON FOR THE THIRD STUD, and neither is drawn yet (#828). Figure 2-10 calls for a Panduit LCD6-14AH-L (or Thomas & Betts 54205UF) 45-degree two-hole lug, and its first step reads "Select either horizontal or vertical mounting": stud-bl and stud-br would be the horizontal landing and stud-tr and stud-br the vertical one. Panduit's 'A' hole-spacing code is 5/8 in., so the pitch is most likely 15.875, not 15.3, but that is a reading of a part number and no held document dimensions the terminal. A pair host across stud-bl and stud-br waits: it would re-grid the terminal and move two of its nested slots under a new key, which is a major, and the pitch it would be drawn at is still an inference.
gaps.wanted: a photograph of the C40G rear lower-left corner, which would settle the count and the pitch together in one look; or a dimensioned drawing of the shelf ground terminal, which would let the horizontal pair become one two-hole landing

gaps.note: The card band runs 37.5 to 386.7 in a body 432.95 wide, so it sits 37.5 from the left edge and 46.25 from the right - 8.75 mm out of centre, or 4.375 on the band's own centreline. Everything inside the band agrees with everything else; the question is whether the band is really off-centre in the metal, and nothing we hold answers it. IT IS NOT COSMETIC, and the AC input panel is where it bites. Its four C14 inlets sit behind the four front power supplies. Reflect the supply centres about the PANEL and the inlets are 1.2 out; reflect them about the CHASSIS - which is what walking round a box actually does - and they are 9.95 out. The gap between those two answers IS this asymmetry, and no arrangement of the parts inside the band can close it, because the disagreement is between the band and the chassis rather than within either. THE SUPPORTING NUMBERS ARE ALSO ODD IN THE SAME DIRECTION. The two front fan strips measure 36.0 wide each - equal, as you would expect - but leave 1.5 outside them on the left and 10.25 on the right. Two equal strips with unequal surrounds is exactly the shape of a band that has been positioned from one edge. NOT RESOLVED BY GUESSING, deliberately. Re-centring the band would move the two fan strips, the card bays on both faces, the PSU row, the PSU cover and the AC panel - and it would be one estimate reconciled against another, which this device's `pem-band-top-edge` note already records going wrong twice in opposite directions.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned C40G front or rear elevation from Casa, or a tape measure across a real chassis from its left edge to the first card slot and from the last card slot to its right edge

gaps.note: The PEM band's BOTTOM edge at 264.5 is agreed by every source and is not in doubt. Its TOP edge is known only to about 2 mm, and the three candidates each have support: 194.0 is the direct reading of Figure 1-4 and is impossible, because the card slot above ends at 194.82; 194.82 is flush against that slot; 196.0 is what the bays carry and is what the manifest now uses, on the argument that 194.82 is an accumulation of six DERIVED slot pitches (426.6 mm over 14 slots on the C100G, carried across) and that the front face shows a measured 1.48 mm margin in the equivalent position. That argument is sound but it is an argument, not a measurement, and the whole disagreement is six pixels at 2.982 px/mm. A tape measure on a real C40G, or any Casa drawing that dimensions the rear panel, would settle it in one number. FIGURE 1-12 HAS NOW BEEN LOOKED AT AND DOES NOT SETTLE IT, recorded so nobody spends the search twice. "C40G power entry module" is the only isolated drawing of this part and the first independent look anything has had at it. Its body measures 866 x 381 px for an aspect of 2.273. The modelled 158.0 x 68.5 is 2.307 and the superseded 158.0 x 70.5 is 2.241, and 2.273 lands 0.04 percent off the midpoint of those two - at 158.0 wide it implies a height of 69.51. IT IS EQUIDISTANT AND CONFIRMS NEITHER. This guide's isolated part drawings are in any case demonstrably about 10 percent wrong about their own aspect - Figure 1-20 draws a card at 12.54 whose real aspect is 11.34 - so a 1.5 percent lean is well inside the drawing's own error. THE NUMBER IS THEREFORE NOT MOVED. It has been moved twice already, in both directions, and a third move on evidence that splits the difference would be the reconciliation loop rather than an escape from it. What Figure 1-12 does confirm is the ARRANGEMENT, which is what a figure is good for: a bolted terminal cover across the top with three fasteners, a minus pair of studs above a plus pair inside two outlined blocks, two release levers standing proud of the body top and bottom, and the yellow disconnect-power label to their right - all of which casa/c40g-pem draws. RECORDED BECAUSE THE MODULE AND THE BAY NOW AGREE, which means nothing will ever flag this again - the fit check that found the original 2 mm discrepancy is satisfied by both being wrong together as easily as by both being right.
gaps.wanted: a dimensioned C40G rear elevation, or a tape measure on the PEM opening

gaps.note: The BDM2/BDM2m datasheet states "Total Power 300 W" in a technical specifications table headed "BDM2/2 m with 6+12 IO Card", whose RF connector row describes that card's six downstream and twelve upstream ports. The figure is the assembly's. A BDM position is TWO modules here - casa/bdm in a front bay and casa/io-6p12 in the paired rear bay, which is why casa/bdm already carries `pairs-with` - and no document we hold divides the 300 W between them. Writing it onto the front module would make the chassis total come out right and the answer to "what does a BDM front module draw" come out wrong, so neither half carries a figure and the chassis total stays a floor. The arithmetic does not settle it either way: 12 x 300 W lands on the C100G's stated 3.6 kW whether the 300 W is the pair or the front half with small rear cards. THE THREE REAR RF I/O CARDS ADDED LATER FALL ON THE SAME SIDE OF THIS AS THE 6+12. casa/rfd, casa/rfu-16x8 and casa/ups-32x4 carry NO power figure, because Tables A-8 and A-9 give their port counts and connector types and no watts at all, and every figure Casa does publish for the slot is already the pair's - Table A-3 heads the DQM column "Maximum consumption with I/O module" and Table A-4 gives "Single DCU w/ RFU I/O" 200 W against "Single DCU w/ RFU UPS 32x4 I/O" 220 W for the same US16x8. Subtracting one from the other to get a rear card's share would be our arithmetic and would also be the wrong subtraction - the 20 W is the difference between two PAIRINGS, not between two I/O cards.
gaps.wanted: a pairable unit that can carry properties, so that a figure measured on a pair can be attached to the pair. The scope is now DATA - every card here declares `power-draw-scope: module-with-paired-io`, so a chassis sum knows not to add the rear partner and L30 catches it if one gains its own figure - but the scope says only THAT the figure covers a pair, not WHICH pair. The C100G HIG gives the same US16x8 200 W with the RFU I/O and 220 W with the RFU UPS 32x4, and the manifest can carry only one of them. Asking for "a per-module figure" was the wrong question: Casa states none, and one may not exist to be divided out. What is missing is the mechanism, and enough vendors doing this to design one from - Casa is the only one in the corpus.

gaps.note: HALF OF THIS IS FIXED. The ASR 9001-S's two licence-disabled SFP+ ports and its disabled modular bay are now stated: roc-ops/Portrayal#193 widened `component-attrs` to accept a placement id as well as a component name, and `bay-attrs` already took a bay path, so sfp-plus-2, sfp-plus-3 and mpa-1 carry `enabled: no` and the licence that unlocks them, in that configuration alone. WHAT IS STILL NOT SAYABLE is the 60 Gbps figure: a configuration can now say what is true of a PART and still cannot override an attr of the DEVICE, so this chassis carries the 120 Gbps switching capacity for both models and the -S's half-capacity lives in prose.
gaps.wanted: a way for a configuration to override a device-level attr - the same widening one level up. docs/what-a-configuration-cannot-say.md now records which two thirds of that shape are closed and why this one is not.

gaps.note: Table 4 of the fixed-port install guide gives the 10MHz and 1PPS connectors as DIN 1.0/2.3. The standards registry has no key for it - sma, smb, mcx and f-type are there, DIN 1.0/2.3 is not - so these two openings are declared as panel cutouts at their measured size rather than composed from a std/ part. Substituting sma or smb would name a connector Cisco does not. THE REASON WAS vendor-silent AND THAT WAS THE WRONG TOKEN. Cisco is not silent - it names the connector outright. What is missing is a panel-cutout dimension, which is needs-drawing, and the difference matters because the two tokens ask different things of a reader: vendor-silent reads as closed until better documents appear, needs-drawing reads as an errand somebody can run today. The correction came from asr9k-cards, who had just been wrong in exactly this direction about the XFP - concluding a figure was unsourceable after searching the intake rather than the standards - and found it in INF-8077i ten minutes after looking somewhere else. IEC 61169-8 is the somewhere else here, and nobody has opened it yet.
gaps.wanted: a std/din-1-0-2-3 part and its standards.yaml key. THE CONNECTOR IS STANDARDISED, so a sourced dimension exists to be found rather than estimated - DIN 1.0/2.3 is specified in IEC 61169-8, and any manufacturer's bulkhead-jack panel drawing carries the D-hole figure. std/mcx is the worked example of exactly this being done properly earlier tonight: registered from IEC 61169-36 / CECC 22220 at 4.95 x 4.50 with confidence verified, replacing an estimate that was 28 percent too small. This should be done the same way, and until it is, an sma or smb standing in would be a plausible wrong answer - which is the failure mode this project keeps having to dig back out

gaps.note: cisco/a9k-pwr-3kw-ac@1 states 142.78 mm wide. Three of them need 428.34 mm and this chassis's power shelf interior measures 416.50, so they do not fit - lint L13 flagged the overlap directly when they were placed at the measured centres. Against that, the stencil's shape box for the 'A9K Power Module' master reads 0.5477 in, which is 139.12 mm at the stencil's 1:10 scale, and my own measurement of the three openings in the ASR 9006 front master gives 138.35, 137.50 and 138.23. Those two agree to under a millimetre, and three at 139.12 come to 417.36 against a 416.50 shelf - the arithmetic a shelf that holds exactly three ought to produce. The 142.78 is most likely the art measured over something that is not the module's seating width, the same class of error as reading a card's shape box instead of its art. The bays here are sized to the measured openings, so the chassis is right and the component and the chassis disagree by about 3.7 mm until someone re-measures the master.

gaps.note: THESE BAY DIMENSIONS WERE GROWN TO MEET A COMPONENT AND ARE NOT MEASUREMENTS. Each was set by taking the size of a card the bay accepts, because a fit check reported the bay as too small. On this chassis: 492.10 on 5 bays - a99-sfc3-s, 492.10 long The ten card bays left this list when they took the family standard, 41.4 x 395.7 (see asr9000-card-standard). The danger is specific and it is why they are listed rather than left to look like geometry. A fit check compares a bay to a component and NEITHER of them to the world, so it is satisfied by both being wrong together exactly as easily as by both being right. These are the entries where that happened, so the record survives the check going quiet. What IS independently grounded and is not in this list: the cage extents, measured off the stencil and confirmed on several chassis by printed slot labels or a card guide rail; the slot pitch; the 395.70 fourth-generation envelope, which is Cisco's own "includes ejector bracket/lever" figure; and the shapesheet sizes for the power modules and fan trays. gaps.note: The guide states that line cards are installed upside down in slots 10 through 19 of the bottom card cage but right side up in slots 0 through 9 of the top card cage. This is a real property of the chassis and the model cannot currently express it. The bays for 10 to 19 are geometrically identical to 0 to 9 and carry no rotation, because the card is inverted about its own long axis rather than rotated in the plane of the panel - a `rotate: 180` would spin the faceplate end for end, which is a different thing and would put the ejectors at the wrong ends. So a card rendered in slot 15 will show its ports and its part number the same way up as one in slot 5, and on real hardware it would not. Anyone reading port positions off the lower cage should know that.

gaps.note: THE REAL MACHINE HAS THREE LEVELS AND THIS MODEL HAS TWO. Overview and Reference Guide, "Cisco ASR 9922 Router Power Modules": "ASR-9922 supports: Four AC PEMs (power shelves). Version 2 supports four power supplies and version 3 supports three power supplies", and for DC "Four DC PEMs. Each PEM supports up to four power supplies." So the chassis holds four shelves and each shelf holds the supplies; this face draws sixteen supply bays directly, which is 4 x 4 flattened. WHAT THAT COSTS IS FOUR SOURCED PARTS WITH NOWHERE TO GO. cisco/a9k-power-tray is the version 2 shelf, cisco/a9k-ac-pem-v3 and cisco/a9k-dc-pem-v3 are the version 3 shelves - all three drawn off stencil masters at 468.12 x 48.03 - and cisco/a9k-power-shelf-cover is the blank for one. They are unplaced because there is no shelf bay to seat them in, not because nobody knows where they belong: the guide names them by PID against this chassis. THE SIXTEEN BAYS ARE NOT WRONG, and this is why the flattening has stood: a version 2 shelf holds four supplies and 4 x 4 is sixteen, so the supply positions are right for the V2 build. They are wrong for V3, which puts three supplies in a shelf - twelve, not sixteen - and that difference is invisible while the shelves are not there. See roc-ops/Portrayal#262.

Calibrated against the rear handle, whose device y is trusted, the convention is face_y = 86.8 - raw_y; it reproduces the handle's low edge at 42.35 to the hundredth and this assembly's own sibling R740XD_Expansioncard_Clip-1.001 at y 1.81..44.81, the figure riser-1-shroud-14g already carried from an independent read. The pose is seated and the 36.9 mm was real all along - a plausibility check that fires on the reader instead of the data rejects good evidence, and it cost a wrong fix at the other end of the part. WHAT THE MODEL ACTUALLY SHOWS, descended to mesh children, is two levels: Body_2_3.002 at 111.70..148.60, 11.06 proud - a wide lower shelf, now drawn - and Body_1_3.005 at 125.00..135.10, 17.71 proud - a narrow rib. WHAT IS STILL OPEN is the rib. riser-1-shroud-14g draws it 120.64..137.26, about 4 mm wider on each side than the body at that depth. The outline came from cad-outline.py cutting at the panel plane, which returns the SILHOUETTE of everything the plane crosses rather than one body, so it cannot settle a single body's width. Re-cutting it would move the slot column and the clip recess, both photo-measured off ISM figure 8 and both currently agreeing with the render, so it is recorded rather than guessed. gaps.note: TWO NUMBERS, ONE APPEARANCE EACH, AND NEITHER CORROBORATED. This device seats both supplies at y 46.20, and the only other place that number appears is a comment on riser 2's plate saying the plate was cut back to "face 46.20 - the power supply's top edge", which cites this seating rather than a source. psu-1100w-ac-14g's provenance used to argue the module top was y 45.0, read off R740 ISM figure 9 - but it argued that in the same breath as a height of 41.8, and the height has since been measured off Dell's own service model at 39.1. THE CAD CANNOT ANSWER IT. glb-parts.py states the rule it enforces: sizes survive a pose and positions do not, and this scene draws the supply with its withdrawal handle swung open for a removal procedure. The body measures cleanly at 86.3 x 39.1 x 195.5 and its face y lands nowhere near either candidate. AN ATTEMPT TO RE-READ FIGURE 9 FAILED GATE 1 AT 13.18%, against a provenance that claims 0.26% for the same figure - so the failure is in the panel detection, not in the figure, and nothing may be taken off it until somebody finds the body's true top and bottom edges in that raster. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the body edges in ISM figure 9 identified by hand rather than by ink-density, which turns the 13.18% back into the 0.26% the figure is capable of and makes the fraction readable. 1.2 mm is worth one careful pass, because riser 2's plate is cut to this number.

gaps.note: DELL ENUMERATES THEM. ISM table 28, "Supported backplane options for PowerEdge R740XD systems", lists front, mid and rear together - ten rows, and the coupling falls straight out: 2.5in x24 no rear 2.5in x24 + 2.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear 2.5in x24 (20 SAS/SATA + 4 NVMe) no rear 3.5in x12 no rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 3.5in x2 rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x4 mid + 2.5in x4 rear 3.5in x12 + 3.5in x2 rear 3.5in x12 + 2.5in x4 rear 2.5in x24 NVMe no rear 3.5in x12 Hybrid with NVMe U.2 no rear The 24-bay front takes ONE rear, the 4 x 2.5 inch, which figure 19 numbers 24-27. The 12-bay front takes either, and figure 19 numbers both from 12. This device carries the 24-bay front, which is why its rear reads 24-27. THE ARITHMETIC GOT THERE FIRST AND IS NOW REDUNDANT. Bays numbered 12-15 imply eleven bays this model does not have; that is how the error was found. Table 28 is how it is now SOURCED, and a guess agreeing with a document afterwards is worth more than either alone. THE RISER SIDE IS TABLE 25, and its discriminator is riser 2 rather than riser 3. Rear storage is offered in riser configurations 0, 1 and 2 and no others: 1 and 2 fit a one-slot low-profile riser 2 (2B or 2C, slot 4 only), while configuration 3 fits a three-slot 2A (slots 4, 5, 6) and has NO rear storage despite fitting no riser 3 at all. It is riser 2's full-height section that occupies the bay the rear cage needs. This device's configurations already encode exactly that - rear storage only with rc0, rc1 and rc2 - and row 3 is `rc3-1a2a`, added when the riser 3 opening and rear storage bay 3 turned out to be the SAME HOLE, closed by two different blanks depending on which configuration you picked. RE-READ AND STILL OPEN: that change touched which bay closes an opening, not the front-to-rear coupling this gap is about. Re-read again when riser 1's brackets moved 1 mm and slot 2 lost its numeral on 1A - both are ink and geometry inside one bay, and neither reaches across faces. Re-read a third time when riser 1's plate grew to meet the slot strip and the shroud: the bay's own box moved, and still nothing crossed a face. A fourth time when riser 2's three slots were aligned and its plate cut back to the full-height pair. That one surfaced a NEW question but not a new gap of this kind: a bay's occupant is drawn after the panel, so a card cannot be shown "only through its cutout" without a part drawn after the bays to mask it. Recorded where it belongs, on the riser 2 slot 6 cutout, rather than widened into this one. A fifth time when the screw tab was split out of the frame so it could draw in front of riser 2's bracket tails. That is a draw-order fact about one bay, not a coupling between faces. A sixth time when riser 3 became bay 1 reflected - mirrored brackets, a two-slot plate and its own slot strip. Handedness is a fact about one bay's own metal and reaches no further than that. A seventh time when riser 3 slid 9.525 right to sit over the power supply's edge. Moving one bay along its own face changes nothing about which front it can be sold with. An eighth time when two "rivet" pairs beside the divider turned out to be card retention clips. A misread of what is on the rear, corrected on the rear, and silent about any front. A ninth time when those rivets came back, scoped: they are what the riser cage mounts to and they show when drives are fitted instead. That one is a rear configuration telling two rear drawings apart, which is the mechanism this gap says is MISSING between faces - and still is. A tenth time when the C20 supply became its own part. A second occupant for an existing bay, on the same face, coupled to nothing at the front. TWO SOURCES DISAGREE AND ARE LEFT DISAGREEING. The system information label draws FIVE fronts - 24, 16 and 8 x 2.5 inch, 12 and 8 x 3.5 inch - where table 28 lists TWO front backplanes. Whether the 16- and 8-bay fronts are different chassis or one backplane drawn part-populated, nothing held here says. AND TABLE 28 HAS A MID DRIVE TRAY in three of its ten rows. This device models no mid bay at all, which is a whole third drive location missing rather than a detail. RE-READ WHEN `ru: 2` WAS STATED (#734), and all nine gaps still open. The chassis had no rack units at all, so its DCIM exports called a 2U server 1U; stating them moves nothing on any face and settles none of these.
gaps.wanted: NOW DEMONSTRABLE RATHER THAN HYPOTHETICAL. `rear-2-lff` draws a correct 2 x 3.5 inch rear on a 24 x 2.5 inch front, and ISM table 28 lists no such machine - every row carrying that rear has a 12-bay front. The mismatch even forced an id: the figure prints 12 and 13, which are already two of this chassis's front bays, so the rear ones had to be rear-drive-12 and rear-drive-13. An id clash is what this gap looks like from the inside. RE-READ AFTER THE REAR BAYS WERE SEPARATED, and still open. The rear half of this is now expressible: the chassis structure across bays 2 and 3 is its own always-present part, and what each bay holds - drives, PCIe, a blank - varies independently of the other. That was the piece `only-in` could not reach while one 287 mm component owned both bays. WHAT REMAINS IS THE FRONT. The 24 x 2.5 inch and 12 x 3.5 inch fronts are different panels, not different occupancy, and until the second is drawn nothing exercises the face-binding that would couple it to a rear. A way for a configuration to constrain more than one view at once. Today `only-in` scopes a bay to a configuration and every view chooses independently, so nothing stops a consumer selecting a 24-bay front and a rear numbered 12-15 - a machine that cannot be bought. The library needs either configurations that span views, or a declared incompatibility between them; and this device needs its 12 x 3.5 inch front modelled before either can be exercised, which is the same gap `rear-2-lff` already stands on.

agr110-datasheet/doc.md:109 states 438.4 x 501.9 x 44 mm and agr110-qsg's hardware specification states 435 x 515 x 43.84 mm. All three axes differ and the depth differs by 13 mm, which is not rounding. The datasheet is modelled, for the reasons in provenance - the sibling's datasheet states the same triple independently, 438.4 is the body width this vendor's 1RU line uses, and the figure's own aspect prefers it - but the quick-start is not wrong for being outvoted, and the same conflict stands unresolved on agr130, which shares that quick-start. A tape measure on a real unit settles it in one minute.

The six QSFP28 ports are numbered 48 to 53 here on the strength of the vendor's zero-based scheme, not on a reading. No figure held resolves their numerals: the quick-start's section 6 zoom crops that end of the faceplate away and the datasheet render prints the band under its own callout highlighting. Which column is the lower number, and whether the separate bottom row continues the sequence or precedes it, need a straight-on photograph of the right-hand end of the front panel.

The bezel between the upper QSFP block's two rows carries FOUR marks per column where the SFP+ bezel carries two. That is either two lamps per port or a four-lane column serving one of them, and 9.1 px/mm cannot separate those. One lamp per port is drawn; the other two marks per column are not. A photograph of one QSFP shell at better than 9 px/mm settles it.

The quick-start's section 6 zoom draws PS0, PS1, Diag, Fan and Loc as text INSIDE a light rectangle, which reads as a legend printed on the lens rather than beside it - unlike Reset, two centimetres away on the same band, which is plain white text on the chassis. It is drawn here as a lamp with its legend over it. Whether the real part prints on the lens or beside it is a bench photograph.

The management jack's link and activity lamps are BELOW THE CONSOLE PORT, not in the jack - a reader with better photographs than this corpus holds sees them there, which is why the jack is modelled on the bare std/rj45-ganged@2 rather than the lamped Ethernet cell. They are now placed, straddling the `Mgmt` label at 409.30 and 420.20 mm, from a reader looking at the hardware. The datasheet render does not resolve them on its own - the band carries marks at 407.88, 409.63 and 410.73 mm and a brighter one at 30.1 to 31.0, and at 9.1 px/mm nothing separates a lamp from a legend among them - so the positions bracket the label rather than landing on a measured mark. What remains open is only the exact offset either side.

Twenty-six lamps on this face carry a legend printed on the lens: the twenty-four lane lamps their lane number 0 to 3, and the two management lamps `LNK` and `ACT` - legible in a close photograph of the hardware. It is not drawn, and the obstacle is the model rather than the evidence: the renderer paints a placement over its own silkscreen, so ink at a lamp's centre is invisible and L21 says so, and there is nowhere else for it to go - the port numerals sit 0.8 mm above the lamp row and the label bar directly below it. The same is true of the five system-LED legends at the other end of the face. What would fix both is a way for a lamp to carry a legend on its own lens, which is a component or renderer question and not this device's to answer.

The two grounding points do not look alike. Callout 7 points to a single round opening at the lower left, about 7.9 mm; the right-hand end carries a light plate with two holes one above the other, 424.7 to 436.7 mm, which matches the quick-start's "One grounding lug, 2 M5 screws" kit. Both are drawn with common/ground-lug@1. Whether the left-hand one is a second lug pad, a single bonding screw, or something else is a photograph of the rear left corner.

agr130-datasheet/doc.md:103 states 438.4 x 501.9 x 44 mm and the quick start guide's hardware specification - the one this model SHARES with the AGR110 - states 435 x 515 x 43.84 mm. All three axes differ and the depth differs by 13 mm, which is not rounding. The datasheet is modelled, for the reasons in provenance - the sibling's datasheet states the same triple independently, 438.4 is the body width this vendor's 1RU line uses, and this model's own figure aspect prefers it - but the quick-start is not wrong for being outvoted, and the same conflict stands unresolved on agr130, which shares that quick-start. A tape measure on a real unit settles it in one minute.

The six QSFP28 ports are numbered 48 to 53 here on the strength of the vendor's zero-based scheme, not on a reading. No figure held resolves their numerals: the quick-start's section 6 zoom crops that end of the faceplate away and the datasheet render prints the band under its own callout highlighting. Which column is the lower number, and whether the separate bottom row continues the sequence or precedes it, need a straight-on photograph of the right-hand end of the front panel.

The bezel between the upper QSFP block's two rows carries FOUR marks per column where the SFP+ bezel carries two. That is either two lamps per port or a four-lane column serving one of them, and 9.1 px/mm cannot separate those. One lamp per port is drawn; the other two marks per column are not. A photograph of one QSFP shell at better than 9 px/mm settles it.

The quick-start's section 6 zoom draws PS0, PS1, Diag, Fan and Loc as text INSIDE a light rectangle, which reads as a legend printed on the lens rather than beside it - unlike Reset, two centimetres away on the same band, which is plain white text on the chassis. It is drawn here as a lamp with its legend over it. Whether the real part prints on the lens or beside it is a bench photograph.

The management jack's link and activity lamps are BELOW THE CONSOLE PORT, not in the jack - a reader with better photographs than this corpus holds sees them there, which is why the jack is modelled on the bare std/rj45-ganged@2 rather than the lamped Ethernet cell. They are now placed, straddling the `Mgmt` label at 409.30 and 420.20 mm, from a reader looking at the hardware. The datasheet render does not resolve them on its own - the band carries marks at 407.88, 409.63 and 410.73 mm and a brighter one at 30.1 to 31.0, and at 9.1 px/mm nothing separates a lamp from a legend among them - so the positions bracket the label rather than landing on a measured mark. What remains open is only the exact offset either side.

Twenty-six lamps on this face carry a legend printed on the lens: the twenty-four lane lamps their lane number 0 to 3, and the two management lamps `LNK` and `ACT` - legible in a close photograph of the hardware. It is not drawn, and the obstacle is the model rather than the evidence: the renderer paints a placement over its own silkscreen, so ink at a lamp's centre is invisible and L21 says so, and there is nowhere else for it to go - the port numerals sit 0.8 mm above the lamp row and the label bar directly below it. The same is true of the five system-LED legends at the other end of the face. What would fix both is a way for a lamp to carry a legend on its own lens, which is a component or renderer question and not this device's to answer.

The two grounding points do not look alike. Callout 7 points to a single round opening at the lower left, about 7.9 mm; the right-hand end carries a light plate with two holes one above the other, 424.7 to 436.7 mm, which matches the quick-start's "One grounding lug, 2 M5 screws" kit. Both are drawn with common/ground-lug@1. Whether the left-hand one is a second lug pad, a single bonding screw, or something else is a photograph of the rear left corner.

WHAT THE DC TERMINAL ACTUALLY IS. The datasheet names it and stops - "DC Inlet: Amphenol Terminal" - with no series, no part number and no drawing, and the guide adds only the wire gauge. So edgecore/agr560-psu-dc@1's block is drawn to the guide's rear elevation at 5.08 px/mm and nothing else: a 18.7 x 31.6 frame with two 10.7 wells on a 13.7 mm stud pitch. THE COUNT IS SAFE - the ordering table's cable is "6AWG PSU to 2 x Ring Terminal", so two studs is stated, not deduced - but the well diameter and the stud size are a round half of a measurement taken to about a quarter of a millimetre. An Amphenol catalogue drawing would replace them outright. The same gap is open on edgecore/ais800-64-psu-dc@1 for the same vendor's six-stud block.

A PHOTOGRAPH THAT SHOWS A SUPPLY LATCH ON THIS MACHINE AT ALL, in either build. Both supplies are drawn with a neutral #3d3d3f tab, and that is a measurement rather than a default: counted over the whole supply column of the datasheet's rear photograph at 9.56 px/mm, the AC build carries 133 red pixels - a 1.2 mm streak that is the red wire behind the fan guard - against the fan trays' 106,257 on the same face, and the module's right margin reads a flat dark grey. The guide's rear elevation, which is the only document that draws the DC build, cannot help: it renders both supplies with ZERO saturated pixels while colouring the trays' handles on the same drawing. SO THE HONEST READING IS THAT THE TAB IS NOT A COLOURED PART, and the AIS800 family's airflow-colour convention is not evidence here - that family ships in two airflows and photographs both, and this machine ships front-to-back only. Both components were first written with that family's red and green and both were corrected. What would close this is one clear photograph of either supply's right edge out of the chassis.

THE PERFORATION PATTERNS, PITCHES AND EXTENTS, which are the softest numbers on this face. The panel carries two styles - honeycomb along the top and bottom of the port wall and at the right-hand corners, and short slots above and below each QSFP-DD block - and both were found by clustering a local-variance map of a textured photograph rather than measured. The field RECTANGLES are good to about a millimetre; the pitches are estimates chosen to look right at 5 px/mm and are not read off anything. They are drawn because a panel with blank metal where perforation is would be wrong in a more misleading way than one whose hole pitch is approximate, but nothing here should be treated as measured. A mechanical drawing, or a photograph at 15 px/mm, closes it.

Which end of the rear the fan trays number from. The chassis silkscreens a mark on the rail beside each bay, and at the source's real resolution it cannot be read: the rear elevation is embedded in the PDF at 1.83 px/mm, where a 2 mm numeral is 3.7 pixels. gaps.note: TWO EDGECORE DOCUMENTS GIVE THIS CHASSIS TWO DEPTHS, 61 mm apart. The data sheet (Edgecore AGR100 (AS5912-54X) Data Sheet R20) states 440 x 548 x 44 mm (W x D x H). gaps.note: The datasheet states "Power Consumption - Max: 527 W, Typical: 186 W" with no ambient. The quick start guide for the same SKU states "Power Consumption 638 W at 25 C, 695 W at 45 C". This is not the usual measure-versus-measure difference that explains most such pairs: the QSG's LOWEST figure, at the cooler ambient, already exceeds the datasheet's stated MAXIMUM by 111 W, so neither typical-against-max nor an ambient axis accounts for it. Both rows are labelled Power Consumption and neither states a scope or a population. 527 W is kept because it is the datasheet's, which is the source of record for a spec-table fact; if the QSG is right the device draws 21 percent more than this manifest says.
gaps.wanted: a measurement from a running unit, or any Edgecore document stating what each figure covers - populated or bare, input power or system draw. Note that the AGR420's QSG gives 527 W at 25 C, the same number this datasheet gives as the AGR400's maximum, which may mean one of the four figures is a copy error

gaps.note: Searched and absent, which is why this is asserted rather than left to L27 to imply. Both documents we hold - the datasheet and the QSG - rate the AGR PSUs by INPUT only ("DC Input: -40 to -75V, 40 A, per PS"; "AC Input: 100-120 V 12 A or 200-240 V 7.5 A per PS") and state no output wattage anywhere. The fan module gets no power figure at all. Unlike the Casa PEMs, these PSUs genuinely CONVERT, so `power-output-w` is the right key for them and the only thing missing is the number - which is exactly why it must not be derived from the input current, where 12 A at 100-120 V and 7.5 A at 200-240 V give different products and neither is an output rating.

gaps.note: The datasheet states "Power Consumption - Max: 692 W, Typical: 201 W" with no ambient. The QSG for the same SKU states "527 W at 25 C, 723 W at 45 C". Most of that is explained by ambient rather than by disagreement - 527 W at 25 C sits comfortably below the datasheet maximum - but the 45 C figure EXCEEDS the stated maximum by 31 W, and 45 C is the top of this device's own rated operating range (0 to 45 C), so the figure at that ambient should BE the maximum. 692 W is kept as the datasheet's own maximum.

WHICH OF A QSFP28 PORT'S THREE LAMPS SHOWS WHICH BREAKOUT LANE. The quick start guide's Status LEDs panel states colours by SPEED and not by lamp - 'QSFP28 Port LEDs: Blue - 100G, Yellow - 40G, Cyan - 2 x 50G, Magenta - 4 x 25G, Green - 4 x 10G' - and never says how many lamps a port has, let alone what each one means. The face draws three, and a 4 x 25G or 4 x 10G breakout has four lanes, so the obvious one-lamp-per-lane reading cannot be right. The lamps carry the library's off/on default and no legend is invented. A LED table naming the lamps, or a bench photograph of one port under a known breakout, settles it.

WHICH FABRIC PORT EACH LAMP OF A BLOCK'S TWO-LAMP COLUMN BELONGS TO. Each fabric block carries a vertical pair of lamps at its inboard edge, one pair per row, serving that row's two ports. Nothing in either document says which lamp is which port, and at 2.27 px/mm the lamps are 2 px across with no legend beside them. Each pair is therefore drawn `for:` BOTH of its ports rather than one lamp being assigned to each, because assigning them would be a guess wearing a measurement's clothes. A photograph of the fabric block at 5+ px/mm settles it.

THE OUTLINE OF EACH AIR-FILTER COVER AND THE POSITIONS OF ITS CAPTIVE SCREWS. The filter is a real field-replaceable assembly - the guide gives it a three-step procedure: loosen the cover's captive screws, swap the old filter for a new one, then refit the cover and tighten the captive screws - and the Overview numbers it as item 3. What is NOT resolvable is where one cover ends and the next begins: the mesh WINDOWS measure cleanly but a cover's own edge is a shadow line a pixel wide, and the screw heads sit in the top strip where the filter media's texture defeats every threshold that finds a smooth disc elsewhere on the face. The filters are therefore drawn as the vent fields they present rather than as seated FRU components. A mechanical drawing, or a straight-on photograph of the front at 5+ px/mm, would settle it.

THE FACEPLATE OF THE 48 VDC SUPPLY. The datasheet offers '48 VDC Power Supply: Input Voltage: 40 to 72 VDC' beside the AC one, but both staged documents draw and photograph only the AC machine - the guide's Overview calls out '8. 2 x AC PSUs' and both rear elevations show C14 inlets. There is no DC face to model, so no cor550-psu-dc part was written, and the dc-f2b configuration seats the AC part - wrong at the connector, which is what this gap and lint L120 keep in view until a DC face turns up.

THE VENDOR ORDERING CODES FOR THE AC SUPPLY AND THE FAN TRAY. The datasheet's ordering table lists chassis SKUs only (carried on the configurations), and the guide's replacement procedures name no part. Both FRUs are therefore named for the chassis, which library/components/README.md allows only because no model number exists to use instead. If a COR550 ordering table lands, both parts should be renamed to their FRUs and this device should take the major that costs - edgecore/fan-2u-1x1sn@1 is the precedent for both the rename and its price.

WHETHER EACH TRAY CARRIES ONE FAN OR TWO IN SERIES. The datasheet says '4+1 redundant, hot-swappable fan modules' and 'Fans: Hot-Swappable 4+1 redundant fans' and never gives a fan count. One rotor is visible through each tray's mesh. This vendor's other 2RU trays carry two in series and say so in words - edgecore/fan-2u-1x1sn@1's datasheets print '4 hot-swappable fan modules (2 fans per module), 8 fans total' - but nothing of the kind is printed for this machine, so the bay count is five and the fan count is not claimed.

A figure or drawing of this faceplate that can carry a dimension. THE ONE THAT EXISTS CANNOT, AND THE PROOF IS A STANDARD IT CONTRADICTS. Its SFP cage pitch reads 14.7-14.75 measured two ways - across the four cage bores and across the shell walls between them - against the SFF-8432 figure of 14.25 that the registry carries and that the CSR200's figure reproduces at 14.22. Its RJ-45 cell pitch reads 14.4 against a registry 13.97, the same three percent high. And its DC terminal blocks read about eleven percent SMALL against the sibling's. Nothing reconciles those with one scale. THE OBVIOUS EXPLANATION WAS TESTED AND FAILED. A perspective render would taper: panel height sampled along x is flat on both faces, 425-419 px across the CSR200 and 425-430 across this one, and the CSR180's absolute feature POSITIONS line up with the CSR200's to a millimetre or two over the whole 440. What is wrong is local scale, not geometry - the art is honeycomb dark-on-dark at low contrast and repeated careful reads of one feature wobble by 0.5 to 1 mm where the CSR200's repeat to 0.05. WHAT WAS DONE ABOUT IT: every standard part takes its size from the registry - SFP 14.25, RJ-45 13.97, USB-A, SMB - and the figure supplies POSITIONS and COUNTS only. That is the division docs/modelling-a-device.md already draws for ganged pitch, applied to the whole face. The two non-standard parts, common/dc-terminal-24@1 and edgecore/filter-slot-5915-16x@1, are sized from edge POSITIONS for the same reason, and each says so.

Which of the four stacked RJ-45 positions is which. The face carries two 1x2 stacks - four jacks - and the datasheet names only THREE non-traffic RJ-45s: the console (callout 4), the ToD/1PPS (callout 10) and the management port (callout 11). There is no BITS port on this model, which is the CSR200's callout 4 and the reason that device has twelve callouts and this one eleven. The silkscreen under the left stack is a single lamp and legend where the CSR200 has two, and it is not legible at 9.63 px/mm. So the fourth position is either blank or something unlisted, and the three that are named are placed here in the CSR200's order - console top right, management bottom right, ToD/1PPS bottom left - which is an INFERENCE FROM THE SIBLING, not a reading.

A way to print six different numbers from one contract. Each fan module's left-hand strip carries its bay number and a small airflow arrow - the rear elevation shows 1 to 6 at 17.1, 67.5, 117.3, 167.7, 217.0 and 267.4 - and they are printed ON THE MODULE, not on the chassis behind it. edgecore/csr440-fan@1 is one contract used six times, so it cannot carry six digits; drawing them as chassis silkscreen puts them under the module that covers them, which L21 correctly reports as printing on nothing. SO THEY ARE NOT DRAWN, and the numbering lives in the bay ids `fan-1` to `fan-6`, which is where a consumer reads it anyway. A configuration's `skins:` maps one skin per COMPONENT rather than per bay, so the fix is either six near-identical contracts or a per-bay skin the format does not have. Neither is worth one digit today; this records that the marks exist and why the drawing omits them.

A drawing of the lid, the underside and the two side walls. Neither staged document draws any of them flat: the quick start's mounting figures show the lid and one side in three-quarter view while brackets are being screwed on, which is enough to see that nothing is printed or punched there and not enough to model. Each of the four therefore carries an `empty:` sentence saying where I looked, per docs/deliberately-empty-faces.md - EMPTY BY VERIFICATION, not by omission. L45 STILL WARNS ABOUT THEM AND THIS GAP IS WHAT ANSWERS IT, because that rule exempts a view a gap names rather than one carrying an `empty:` sentence. Worth saying plainly: the CSR440 clears the same rule only because an unrelated chassis-weight gap happens to scope all six views, which the rule's own comment calls over-exemption; this one names the four faces because they are what it is about. IT DOES NOT COST THE DEVICE ITS CAPABILITY LEVEL. I asserted that it did and was wrong - the grader reads six views here and the 3D build is whole. A mechanical drawing would still improve these four faces from honest blanks to drawn ones.

What the last two white legend boxes say. The label strip carries six bracketed groups of four - the breakout lane legend, one bracket per QSFP28 port, and they read 49 to 54 in order - and then TWO MORE boxes of the same size and pitch at 362.98 and 369.01 mm, under the numerals for ports 47 and 48, belonging to no bracket. At 5 px/mm their contents are not legible and no table in either document accounts for a seventh pair. They are left undrawn rather than guessed, and this gap is the record that they exist and where.

An orthographic elevation, or a mechanical drawing. The only full-panel figures this corpus holds are perspective renders: the top cover is drawn above the face and the face tapers 0.9% from its top edge to its bottom. That costs the vertical axis entirely - every y on both faces is constructed from the registry's row pitch and the family's idiom rather than read - and it leaves the horizontal axis with a 0.84% residual against the stated width, which is why the panel is 442.5 because two documents say so rather than because the drawing shows it. A flat elevation would settle the row positions, the label-strip height and the width residual in one pass.

A way to print a numeral and its direction arrow together. Each of the 48 SFP+ numerals is drawn on the metal as a digit followed by a small up or down triangle - "1 up", "2 down" - naming which row of the column the port is in. Block expansion generates the digit and has no vocabulary for the glyph beside it, and hand-writing 48 marks to add it would take the whole block out of generation for one triangle each. A FAN FRU NUMBER FOR THIS MODEL. `edgecore/dcs520-fan@1` was written as its own part and it very probably is not one: the three other devices on this shell all seat a tray whose FRU number `FAN-2U-1x1SN-F` is printed in all three of their datasheets, and this machine's trays sit on a mean pitch of 85.58 against their uniform 85.71 - thirteen hundredths of a millimetre - with the same honeycomb, the same angled red bar with two pairs of slots and a central button, and the same corner lamp. THE MEASUREMENTS ARGUE FOR ONE PART MEASURED TWICE, NOT FOR TWO PARTS. The three gaps here run 85.54, 85.64 and 85.55, a spread of a tenth of a millimetre, where the other three chassis repeat 85.71 with no spread at all; and this face is 80.1 x 83.5 `measured` against the shared tray's 81.6 x 81.2 `photo-measured`, a disagreement of 1.5 x 2.3 mm. Irregular spacing and a face that misses by more than the pitch does are what pixel-measuring a drawing produces beside a dimensioned source. Two rulers, not two trays. NEITHER DCS520 DOCUMENT PRINTS A FAN PART NUMBER, so the argument that settled the other three is unavailable, and the drawings cannot settle it either: scaled to a common size and normalised, 46% of pixels differ by more than a standard deviation, but that is this guide drawing the tray bright with the rotor showing through the mesh against the AIS800 guides drawing it dark. A test that cannot tell a different part from different lighting decides nothing. One FRU list closes this. If it names `FAN-2U-1x1SN-F`, delete this component and seat the shared one.

The slot left of port 0 is one light-pipe opening (photographed square-on), and the vendor's UI view draws four lamps in a column there; all four carry `for: chassis`. The maintainer counts one lamp per 100G port, and the photograph shows no lamp anywhere else near the ports, so two of the four are probably those - but nothing says which, and an invented mapping would be worse than none. Printing 48-51 would put ink on the drawing that is not on the metal, which is the one thing silkscreen must never do - so they are left off, and this entry exists so that a reader comparing the render against the photograph can tell a deliberate absence from an unfinished model.
